tldr: Heavy, expensive motors are consolidated into a base unit, and a detachable mechanism called the "Wire Detach Unit" physically splits and reconnects the wire drive transmission paths. Using a single shared set of actuators, the authors demonstrated interchangeable driving and control of a rigid arm, a continuum arm, and two types of grippers.
hero_caption: Physical appearance of the module set developed in this study. A 2-DOF rigid arm (top left) and a multi-DOF continuum arm (top right) can be interchangeably attached to the shared motor unit at the top, and a multi-finger hand (bottom left) or a parallel gripper (bottom right) can be mounted at the end-effector. In the center is the "Wire Detach Unit," the key device that mechanically splits and couples the wire paths.
overview:
Reconfigurable robots that change their morphology to match the workspace or task offer great versatility. However, mounting dedicated actuators on every module leads to a serious dilemma: overall system weight, volume, and cost soar dramatically. Actuators such as motors account for 30% to 50% of a robot's total weight and cost, making it extremely inefficient to give each module its own motors.

The authors focused on the advantages of "wire drive" systems, which consolidate actuators into a base to reduce weight. However, conventional wire-driven robots use single continuous wires running from the base to the joints, making it fundamentally impossible to attach, detach, or swap modules along the way. To overcome this hurdle, they conceived the "Wire Detach Unit," which mechanically splits and reconnects wire power transmission paths.

In this study, using this detach unit as a building block, the authors built the "Detachable Wire Drive" system. It interchangeably mounts and drives a 2-DOF rigid arm, a flexible continuum arm, a parallel gripper, and a multi-finger gripper from a common motor unit. Experiments confirmed tension transmission up to 450 N and low-friction coupling, and demonstrated smooth posture control and object manipulation while swapping modules.
contributions: Proposed and developed the "Wire Detach Unit," a mechanism that physically separates and reconnects wire power transmission paths with high stiffness and repeatability.
Established the "Detachable Wire Drive" robot architecture, which centralizes heavy motors and control circuits at the base to completely share actuators across different skeletal morphologies.

Demonstrated an integrated framework that drives fundamentally different structures—a rigid arm and a continuum arm—as well as multiple grippers using the same motor set, uniformly estimating and controlling joint angles from wire displacement.

sections.heading: Why take a wire-driven robot apart?
sections.summary: Actuators are the biggest bottleneck for cost and weight in reconfigurable robots. By adding detachment capabilities to wire drives with base-concentrated motors, this work aims for an extremely lightweight, low-cost reconfigurable system.
sections.details:
Reconfigurable robots that alter their structure are widely studied as an approach to adapt to various tasks. They broadly fall into distributed types composed of numerous tiny modules (like M-TRAN) and centralized types with distinct roles, such as tool changers. In terms of practicality, centralized systems excel in stiffness and output. However, they require dedicated actuators inside each module, resulting in poor parts reusability and making the overall system heavy and expensive. Actuators make up 30% to 50% of the entire robot's weight and cost, so sharing them is the key.

This study proposes a centralized approach where actuators are gathered into a shared base unit and power is routed to each part via wires. Compared to hydraulics (fluid leakage risk) or pneumatics (limited control accuracy), wire drives save space, route flexibly, and simplify sensor wiring because joint states can be estimated from wire displacement. Until now, wire-driven robots traditionally relied on a single long wire running throughout, and disconnecting them midway was considered impossible. The authors successfully combined the lightweight benefits of wire drives with the flexibility of reconfigurable robots by developing the "Wire Detach Unit," which mechanically splits and reconnects wire paths.

sections.heading: The core mechanism for reconnecting wires and the diverse module designs
sections.summary: The authors developed a detach unit that relays wire power through clutch-equipped pulleys. Using this unit, they designed a module set combining a shared motor base, a 2-DOF rigid arm, a continuum arm, and two grippers with one-touch mechanical and dynamic coupling.
sections.details:
The entire system consists of a base motor unit, two arms (a 2-DOF rigid arm and a continuum arm), and two end-effectors (a parallel gripper and an underactuated multi-finger gripper), with detach units embedded at each interface.

- **Wire Detach Unit**: Consists of a pulley that winds the wire (high-strength Vectran fiber), guide pulleys for stable winding, a relay point, and male/female clutch teeth that transmit rotational torque (designed with rounded corners for easy engagement). Housed in a fan-shaped outer shell, up to six units can be arranged circumferentially.

- **Motor Unit and Motor-Arm Detacher**: The base unit houses four quasi-direct drive (QDD) motors. Pulleys with a 16 mm radius deliver a continuous tension of up to 312 N and a winding speed of 0.44 m/s. The arm connection uses a latch structure where radial pins on the arm side are elastically locked by a ring on the base side, enabling attachment by just pushing in, and detachment by twisting the outer ring and pulling.

- **Rigid Arm and Continuum Arm**: The rigid arm has two degrees of freedom at the shoulder and elbow, routing three drive wires and an end-effector tool wire (via a Bowden cable). The continuum arm comprises seven unit cells combining springs and restraint sheets, enabling flexible bending motion with infinite degrees of freedom. Three wires control its overall bending.

- **Two End-Effectors**: The authors built a simple parallel gripper with two linearly translating jaws, and an underactuated multi-finger gripper whose three fingers wrap conformally around objects by pulling a single wire. Both can be quickly swapped and attached manually to the arm tip's detacher.

captions.F3: Overall configuration of the proposed "Detachable Wire Drive" system. A rigid arm or a continuum arm attaches to the shared motor unit at the top, and two types of grippers attach to the arm tip. Power transmission as well as wire feed displacement information are transferred through this path.
captions.F4: Internal structure of the "Wire Detach Unit," the core of the power relay. Clutch teeth with male and female profiles are provided on the end face of the wire winding pulley. By engaging with other units or the motor shaft, rotational power is reliably transmitted even though the wire is physically separated midway.
captions.F5: Mechanism details of the "motor-arm detacher" connecting the motor unit and the arm base. Multiple detach units and radial pins are lined up on the arm side (male), and pushing them into the spring-loaded outer ring on the motor side (female) creates a rigid lock with one touch.

sections.heading: Predicting bends without encoders! Unified posture estimation and control
sections.summary: Four control states (ATTACH, CALIBRATE, CONTROL, FREE) manage module swaps. Without angle sensors at the arm joints, joint angles are estimated by optimization calculations from wire winding displacements, and wire tensions are inversely solved from target torques for tracking.
sections.details:
To uniformly control modules even when their skeletal morphology changes drastically, the authors built a control system based on clear state transitions and wire displacements.

- **State Transition**: The system moves among four states: "ATTACH" slightly rotates the motors with low gains to engage the clutches during coupling; "CALIBRATE" sets the wire length origin by letting the arm hang under gravity or pressing it against mechanical limits; "CONTROL" tracks target trajectories; and "FREE" zeroes tension for safe detachment.

- **Joint Angle Estimator**: Weight is strictly minimized by eliminating encoders at the joints. By solving an optimization problem that minimizes the error between geometric wire lengths $\bm{l}$ obtained from motor angles $\bm{\theta}$ and the kinematics function $\bm{H}(\bm{q})$, the estimated joint angles $\hat{\bm{q}}$ are calculated. In underactuated mechanisms with infinite degrees of freedom like the continuum arm, this is not uniquely determined; thus, stable estimation is achieved by imposing a constraint where identical repeating unit cells all bend at equal angles (master-slave relationship).

- **Joint Angle Follower**: Target joint torques $\bm{\tau}_{ref}$ are calculated by summing PID, gravity compensation, and elastic compensation based on the deviation between estimated and target angles. Using this along with the tendon Jacobian $\bm{G}$ (the matrix representing the geometric moment arm through which wire tension converts into joint torque), the target wire tensions $\bm{f}_{ref}$ are solved via quadratic programming optimization under tension upper/lower limits, and converted into motor torque commands.

sections.heading: From tensile strength to arm and hand swapping: hardware validation
sections.summary: Standalone strength and friction tests, arm swap control tests, grasping tests with gripper swaps, and tracking evaluations with AprilTags were performed. The system withstood 450 N tension and performed stable grasping and tracking while swapping modules in about 1 to 10 seconds.
sections.details:
Four experiments were conducted to evaluate the system from multiple angles.

- **Unit Strength and Friction Test**: A detach unit was placed between a motor and a force gauge, cycling tension between 0 and 450 N, and it withstood the load without damage. Input-output tension deviation (friction loss) remained at an average of about $\pm 16$ N, which was confirmed to be small enough for practical use.

- **Continuous Arm Swap and Control Experiment**: A seamless sequence was executed on the motor base: attach rigid arm $\rightarrow$ calibrate $\rightarrow$ angle tracking control $\rightarrow$ detach $\rightarrow$ attach continuum arm $\rightarrow$ calibrate $\rightarrow$ angle tracking control. Attachment took about 10 seconds for clutch engagement, while detachment by turning the ring took only about 1 second. Both arms successfully tracked target angles.

- **End-Effector Swapping and Grasping Experiment**: The parallel gripper and multi-finger gripper were swapped at the tip of the rigid arm (detachment/attachment took about 1 second each). The parallel gripper grasped cardboard boxes and aluminum frames, while the multi-finger gripper conformed to and stably gripped glue sticks and baskets, successfully transporting and releasing them.

- **Rigid Arm Tracking Performance Evaluation**: Actual joint angles were measured using an external camera and AprilTags, and compared with estimated and target values (stepping through 225 joint angle patterns). Estimated angles matched actual angles with high accuracy (RMSE evaluation), proving that posture estimation and feedback control from wire winding displacements achieve sufficient precision.

sections.heading: Clear strengths and the inherent challenges of wire drives
sections.summary: A 450 N load capacity, low friction, one-touch detachment, and operational versatility with a shared controller were demonstrated. Meanwhile, challenges also emerged, including modeling errors from wire deflection and micro-vibrations stemming from a slow 50 Hz control rate.
sections.details:
Experimental results proved that the developed detach unit does not fail even under high tensions of 450 N, with minimal force transmission loss due to friction. Furthermore, operating kinematically distinct rigid and continuum arms with the same motor base and control framework is a powerful advantage of this architecture. In addition, the arm coupling took longer (about 10 seconds) than swapping the end-effector (about 1 second) because the arm side had to engage six pulley clutches simultaneously, whereas the tool side only relayed a single wire line.

On the other hand, slight vibrations and overshoot were observed during rigid arm tracking. The authors attribute this not just to gain tuning, but to two factors. First, "kinematic model errors": the model treats the wire winding start position as a point and neglects wire elongation, slack, and thinning under tension. Second, "control delay": calling geometric calculation functions multiple times within the optimization loop slows the control loop to about 50 Hz. To control wire-driven systems prone to slack and tension without vibration, faster posture estimation algorithms must be introduced to increase the control frequency.

sections.heading: A next-generation robot architecture born from actuator sharing
sections.summary: "Detachable Wire Drive" physically separates and reconnects wire paths, establishing a new design methodology that consolidates and shares motors at the base. It paves the way toward lightweight, low-cost robot platforms adaptable to diverse tasks.
sections.details:
This paper proposed the "Detachable Wire Drive," which shares actuators across distinct robot morphologies to achieve drastic weight and cost reductions across the entire system. Its core, the "Wire Detach Unit," realizes the detachment of power transmission paths with high strength and repeatability, which was impossible in conventional wire drives.

Through hardware experiments using a shared motor unit, two arms, and two end-effectors, the authors validated the mechanical reliability of the mechanism and the effectiveness of software that uniformly estimates and controls postures from wire displacements. Although micro-vibrations remain due to modeling errors and control rate limits, this work demonstrates that actuators can be consolidated and shared using wire drives, offering highly valuable guidance for developing future multi-functional and economical robotic systems.

takeaways: An ingenious mechanical design approach that breaks the conventional wire-drive assumption that "wires cannot be disconnected midway" by using clutch-equipped relay pulleys (Wire Detach Units).

Eliminates encoders on the arm side and estimates joint angles by solving inverse kinematics optimization from motor winding displacements, achieving extreme arm lightweighting and wireless/sensor-free joints.

A versatile control architecture that uniformly handles mathematically distinct structures—a rigid arm and a continuum arm—in a single control pipeline using master-slave constraints and tendon Jacobians.
limitations: Geometric estimation errors appear as micro-vibrations because wire slack and tension-induced diameter changes are modeled as simple point contacts.
Optimization computation limits the control frequency to about 50 Hz, requiring further algorithm acceleration to suppress elastic wire vibrations.
Connecting the motor to the arm requires a waiting time of about 10 seconds for low-speed rotation alignment until all six circumferential clutch teeth engage.
